title: Kerala-Born Nithya Raman Ties Karen Bass in Los Angeles Mayor Race
excerpt: Tied at 40 percent in the final poll before Tuesday's vote, the Indian American councilmember is fighting the mayor, the establishment — and a split inside her own socialist movement.
body:
• Los Angeles votes on Tuesday, November 3: a final UC Berkeley IGS poll co-sponsored by the Los Angeles Times has Mayor Karen Bass and Councilmember Nithya Raman tied at 40 percent each, with 19 percent undecided.
  • Raman, 45, was born in Kerala and moved to the US as a child; a win would make her the first Indian American mayor of Los Angeles.
  • Her own movement is split: DSA's Los Angeles chapter endorsed her, but national DSA leaders have weighed revoking that support over her position on the BDS movement.
  • Raman's strength is young voters — she leads heavily among voters under 40 — but early ballot returns from those age groups have lagged far behind older voters.

The fight for Los Angeles City Hall has become a proxy war over the future of the Democratic Party — and its most closely watched figure is a Kerala-born city councilmember who is simultaneously leading the charge against the party establishment and fighting to keep her own movement's endorsement.

Nithya Raman, 45, an urban planner and former nonprofit executive, is challenging Mayor Karen Bass in Tuesday's November 3 election. A final UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies poll, co-sponsored by the Los Angeles Times and conducted October 19–25, found the two tied at 40 percent among likely voters, with 19 percent undecided, according to reporting by IANS and USA Today. In the same poll in September, Raman led by 11 points, 39 to 28. Bass closed the gap in part by winning over voters who had backed reality television personality Spencer Pratt in the June 2 primary — Pratt voters favoured Bass by 41 percent to 14 percent.

A race about a city in a rut

""We can stop city hall from being a barrier to opening small businesses and building the housing that we desperately need," she told the Journal."

Bass, the first woman elected mayor of Los Angeles, in 2022, has been weighed down by frustration over homelessness and the fallout from the January 2025 wildfires that ravaged Pacific Palisades. A UCLA Luskin School survey found Los Angeles County residents' perception of their quality of life at its lowest level in more than a decade, with satisfaction lower in 2026 than in 2016 across all nine measured categories, the Wall Street Journal reported.

Raman, who had endorsed Bass for another term before jumping into the race in February, has centred her campaign on protecting tenants, expanding transit and bringing down housing costs, and pushed tighter rent controls while leading the council's housing and homelessness committee. "We can stop city hall from being a barrier to opening small businesses and building the housing that we desperately need," she told the Journal. She describes her approach, in her words to Axios, as "sewer socialism" or "pothole politics": "I just want government to work for the people."

The fight inside her own movement

Raman is affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America, and a win would put DSA-aligned politicians in charge of the two most populous cities in the US, after New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani's victory last November. But the endorsement nearly came apart. DSA's Los Angeles chapter backed Raman in September by 937 votes to 484, with 52 abstentions. National DSA caucuses then challenged that endorsement over her positions on Israel and the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement, and the organisation's National Political Committee adopted resolutions under which Raman faced an October 31 assessment meeting — and, if she has not expressed support for BDS and condemned weapons shipments out of Los Angeles International Airport by January 1, a possible vote on expulsion, the Los Angeles Times reported. DSA-LA co-chair Leslie Chang said the national committee passed its resolutions "without reading the materials we sent them."

Raman has broken with DSA before — she was censured by the LA chapter in 2024 after accepting an endorsement from a pro-Israel political organisation, and she publicly split with the national organisation over its response to the October 7, 2023 attacks. At a Jewish mayoral forum in September she described Israel's war in Gaza as a genocide and called BDS a legitimate form of peaceful protest, while saying it is not part of her platform, and that she would keep the Los Angeles Police Department at its current size.

The turnout question

The arithmetic of Tuesday may come down to age. Raman is backed by 69 percent of likely voters aged 18 to 29 and 74 percent of those aged 30 to 39, against 15 and 16 percent for Bass, according to the Times' reporting of the poll. But as of last Wednesday, only 13 percent of eligible voters aged 18 to 34 had submitted ballots, compared with 47 percent of those over 65, according to research firm Political Data Intelligence. "People are sick of establishment politics and want to see a change in the status quo," Raman campaign spokesperson Liz Garcia told the Times. Bass, 73, has drawn endorsements from billionaire developer Rick Caruso, her 2022 rival, and former mayor Antonio Villaraigosa; Raman has the Sierra Club, actor Mindy Kaling and County Supervisor Lindsey Horvath.

Raman is one of at least 57 Indian American candidates on ballots across the US on Tuesday, a list IANS has compiled that runs from a Massachusetts Senate race to Vivek Ramaswamy's run for governor of Ohio. If she wins in Los Angeles, she would be the city's first Indian American mayor — and the first challenger to defeat an incumbent Los Angeles mayor since 2005.
nri_angle: A Kerala-born councilmember could become Los Angeles' first Indian American mayor on Tuesday, in the most watched of 57 Indian American candidacies on US ballots.
author: Diaspora Desk
